notes: \cpara{States the thesis: trying to manage ``PR'' leads to harmful, confused actions, while protecting one's reputation or honor, the author predicts, goes fine.}
\cpara{Explains that guarding honor or reputation means being known to keep fixed standards, as with the Lannisters paying their debts or a gentleman's duel.}

\clogic{Dueling is the author's own example of honor, and it counts against the claim that safeguarding honor ``will basically go fine.'' Men were killed defending a fixed societal standard of exactly this kind. The post needs to say why honor goes fine in modern settings despite this history, and it does not.}
\cpara{The contrasting definition of PR. PR is defined as having no standards. The comparison is decided here, by definition, not later by argument.}
\cpara{Lists the two steps of managing PR: predict what will upset people, then speak so as not to set it off.}
\cpara{Claims this process is loopier, feeds on imagined fears, and, the author thinks, pushes people toward saying nothing at all.}
\cpara{Gives a sign of the difference: PR seems to need outside experts to obey nervously, while honor is something people can know and choose for themselves.}
\cpara{Suggests replacing talk of navigating PR with talk of defending honor or reputation, and predicts this will make people feel clearer and freer.}

\clogic{The whole post is a prediction, marked ``I predict'' in the first paragraph, with no cases offered. One real example of an organization that switched from ``PR'' to ``reputation'' thinking, and what changed, would do more than any argument here.}
